hints: Focus on what the two solutions have in common and what is truly different, the cations $\text{NH}_4^+$ versus $\text{Na}^+$.
Remember that $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is a sparingly soluble base, so think about which cation could react with and remove $\text{OH}^-$ ions.
Consider which ion can act as an acid by giving away $\text{H}^+$, and how that would pull the dissolving equilibrium to the right.
walkthrough:
**Compare the two solutions**

Think side by side with me. Both solutions contain $\text{Cl}^-$ ions and water, so chloride is not the cause.

The only difference is $\text{NH}_4^+$ versus $\text{Na}^+$, so the explanation must come from the chemistry of the cation.

**Recall the dissolving equilibrium of magnesium hydroxide**

$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is sparingly soluble and sets up this equilibrium:
$$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq)$$
To dissolve more solid, we need to remove $\text{OH}^-$ from solution. This is Le Chatelier thinking.

**Identify the acid behaviour of ammonium**

$\text{Na}^+$ is from a strong base and has no acidic proton, so it just watches. $\text{NH}_4^+$ is the conjugate acid of the weak base $\text{NH}_3$, so it can donate a proton:
$$\text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{NH}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
Removing $\text{OH}^-$ pulls the equilibrium in Step 2 to the right, so the solid dissolves. The overall change is:
$$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) + 2\text{NH}_4^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{NH}_3(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

options.A: Ionic radius similarity does not drive this dissolving. Dissolving here is about removing $\text{OH}^-$ by acid-base reaction, not about size matching or lattice substitution.
options.B: Both $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NaCl}$ are strong electrolytes and dissociate fully in water. Even if dissociation differed, that would not explain selective removal of $\text{OH}^-$.
options.C: It is true that $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ are both isoelectronic with neon (10 electrons), but electron count does not explain solubility in this case. This is a distracting true fact with no link to the $\text{OH}^-$ equilibrium.
options.D: This is correct and lovely chemistry. $\text{NH}_4^+$ acts as a Bronsted-Lowry acid, donating $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{OH}^-$ to make $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This removes $\text{OH}^-$, shifts the $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ equilibrium right, and the solid dissolves. $\text{Na}^+$ cannot do this.
